title: Study Design II — Experimental Studies — Test

mcqs.q: Experimental research is a design in which the researcher:
opts: Deliberately changes one or more conditions and observes the effect on an outcome
Documents a naturally occurring relationship without intervening
Compares group averages across populations
Describes the distribution of a variable at one point in time
mcqs.explain: This controlled change is what separates an experiment from many other forms of empirical research.

mcqs.q: Experimental designs are used mainly to:
opts: Examine causal relationships
Estimate prevalence
Describe a population
Generate hypotheses only
mcqs.explain: The researcher introduces a treatment, intervention, condition or stimulus and measures whether the outcome changes.

mcqs.q: Which set belongs to the PRE-EXPERIMENTAL family?
opts: One-shot case study, one-group pretest-posttest, static group
Pretest-posttest control group, posttest-only control group, Solomon four-group
Time series and multiple time series
Randomized blocks, Latin square, factorial design
mcqs.explain: The second set is true-experimental, the third statistical and the fourth quasi-experimental.

mcqs.q: Which set belongs to the TRUE EXPERIMENTAL family?
opts: Pretest-posttest control group, posttest-only control group, Solomon four-group
One-shot case study and static group
Time series and multiple time series
Latin square and factorial design
mcqs.explain: All three use random assignment with a control group.

mcqs.q: In the one-shot case study design:
opts: A single experimental group is evaluated once after the treatment, with no randomization and no control group
Two randomized groups are compared after treatment
The group is tested before and after the treatment
Two non-randomized groups are compared
mcqs.explain: All observations are conducted exclusively after the treatment has been implemented.

mcqs.q: Why can the one-shot case study prove nothing about the treatment?
opts: There is neither a pre-test nor a control group, so there is nothing to compare the post-test against
The sample is always too large
Randomization was performed incorrectly
The outcome is measured too early
mcqs.explain: Any observed change cannot be attributed to the treatment.

mcqs.q: The one-group pretest-posttest design is described as:
opts: The simplest type of pre-experimental design
A true experimental design
A quasi-experimental design
A statistical design
mcqs.explain: Only the experimental group is selected, with a pre-test before and a post-test after the treatment.

mcqs.q: What is missing from the one-group pretest-posttest design?
opts: A control group
A pre-test
A post-test
A dependent variable
mcqs.explain: It measures the impact of the intervention both before and after, but with no control group.

mcqs.q: In the static group comparison design:
opts: Two groups are used but the selection of groups is non-randomized, with post-test observation only
Two randomized groups are pre-tested and post-tested
A single group is tested before and after
Four groups are used, two with pre-tests
mcqs.explain: Group 1 is treated with the intervention X and group 2 receives no intervention or business as usual.

mcqs.q: In the static group comparison, a difference in post-test scores:
opts: Suggests the effect of the intervention, but the groups may have differed beforehand because they were not randomized
Proves the intervention caused the difference
Is meaningless because there is no post-test
Can only be interpreted with a Solomon design
mcqs.explain: Non-randomized selection is the key weakness of all pre-experimental designs with two groups.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed as a use of pre-experimental designs?
opts: Establishing the efficacy of a new drug for licensing
Exploratory studies of a new area or phenomenon
Pilot studies to test feasibility before larger experiments
Preliminary investigations of relationships between variables
mcqs.explain: Establishing efficacy requires a clinical trial; pre-experimental designs are often the first step in the research process.

mcqs.q: Time-series designs provide insights into how outcomes change over time by:
opts: Measuring the dependent variable at multiple time points before and after the introduction of an intervention
Randomly assigning participants to two arms
Comparing two pre-existing schools
Combining results from published studies
mcqs.explain: They are listed among the uses of pre-experimental design.

mcqs.q: A feasibility study assesses:
opts: Whether a larger-scale experimental study is practical and achievable given the available resources and constraints
Whether the outcome measure is valid
Whether randomization was successful
Whether the effect size is statistically significant
mcqs.explain: Educational research, evaluating teaching methods in real-world settings, is another listed use.

mcqs.q: The single feature that distinguishes a TRUE experiment from a pre-experimental or quasi-experimental design is:
opts: Random assignment of participants
The presence of a post-test
The presence of a pre-test
The use of statistical analysis
mcqs.explain: True experimental design employs random assignment, control groups and experimental groups to minimize bias.

mcqs.q: True experimental design is often called the gold standard of research because:
opts: It helps organizations and researchers prove what really drives change
It is the cheapest design available
It requires the fewest participants
It can be completed most quickly
mcqs.explain: Random assignment plus control groups minimizes bias and yields credible results.

mcqs.q: The pretest-posttest control group design:
opts: Measures the dependent variable before and after introducing the independent variable, with only the experimental group receiving the treatment
Takes only a post-test measurement
Uses four groups
Does not randomize participants
mcqs.explain: Both the control and the experimental group are tested.

mcqs.q: The advantage of including a pre-test in a controlled design is that it:
opts: Establishes that the two groups really did start equal and allows change within each group to be measured
Removes the need for randomization
Eliminates the placebo effect
Increases the sample size
mcqs.explain: Without it, only the final between-group difference can be assessed.

mcqs.q: In the posttest-only control group design, participants are:
opts: Randomly assigned to an active treatment or a placebo, and only a post-test measurement is taken
Assigned by the investigator's judgement
Tested before and after the treatment
Given both treatments in random order
mcqs.explain: If the experimental group's results differ from the control group's, cause and effect is established.

mcqs.q: The pre-test can safely be omitted in a randomized design because:
opts: Randomization alone already makes the groups comparable, and omitting it avoids the pre-test influencing participants
Pre-tests are always unreliable
Post-tests are more sensitive
Ethics committees forbid pre-tests
mcqs.explain: This is precisely what the posttest-only control group design exploits.

mcqs.q: The Solomon four-group design:
opts: Combines pretest-posttest and posttest-only designs, using four groups — two with pretests and two without
Uses four randomized groups all with pre-tests
Uses four non-randomized groups
Is a quasi-experimental design
mcqs.explain: The two groups without pre-tests are what allow pretest effects to be controlled.

mcqs.q: What can the Solomon four-group design uniquely reveal?
opts: Both the effect of the research and whether taking a pre-survey influenced the response
The prevalence of the outcome in the population
The incidence rate in the exposed group
Whether the sample is representative
mcqs.explain: No other design can separate the treatment effect from the pre-test effect.

mcqs.q: Quasi-experimental design is used to estimate the causal impact of an intervention but:
opts: Lacks random assignment of participants to experimental and control groups
Lacks a control group entirely
Lacks any outcome measurement
Lacks an intervention
mcqs.explain: Researchers instead work with pre-existing groups or natural cohorts.

mcqs.q: Quasi-experimental designs are especially useful:
opts: In real-world settings where randomization is impractical or unethical
When the sample size is very large
When the outcome is rare
When the intervention is a drug
mcqs.explain: They use pre-existing groups or natural cohorts rather than randomized ones.

mcqs.q: In the quasi-experimental teaching-method example, why is the conclusion limited?
opts: The groups were not randomly assigned and may differ in other ways, such as prior knowledge or demographics
The outcome was not measured
There was no control group
The sample was too small
mcqs.explain: Students from School A used the new method and students from School B did not.

mcqs.q: In the classical RCT structure, after randomization:
opts: One arm is given the intervention and the other is given nothing or a placebo, and both are followed up for the outcome
Both arms receive the intervention in turn
Only the intervention arm is followed up
The outcome is measured before the intervention only
mcqs.explain: In the herbs example, both arms are then counted for influenza or no influenza.

mcqs.q: In the described randomisation process, the computer:
opts: Gives each participant a code number, and the code numbers are randomly assigned to the different treatment arms
Selects which participants are eligible
Chooses the outcome measure
Determines the sample size
mcqs.explain: This helps to prevent bias; the control arm then receives the standard treatment and the test arm the new treatment.

mcqs.q: Blinding refers to:
opts: Patients and investigators, including those recruiting and assessing the outcome, having no knowledge of treatment allocation
The participants being unaware that a study is taking place
The statistician analysing anonymised data
The ethics committee not knowing the sponsor
mcqs.explain: Blinded RCTs are traditionally classified as single-blind, double-blind or triple-blind.

mcqs.q: In a double-blind trial, who is unaware of the allocation?
opts: The patient and the investigator
The patient only
The patient, the investigator and those assessing the outcome
The statistician only
mcqs.explain: Triple-blind additionally conceals allocation from those assessing the outcome.

mcqs.q: Randomization and blinding remove different problems:
opts: Randomization removes bias in who gets what; blinding removes bias in how the result is reported and judged
Randomization removes confounding; blinding removes the need for a control group
Randomization removes measurement error; blinding removes selection error
They both address exactly the same bias
mcqs.explain: This is why a strong trial uses both.

mcqs.q: In a crossover trial:
opts: Each subject usually receives two treatments in random order, often separated by a washout period
Participants are divided into two permanent arms
Only one treatment is given per participant
Randomization is not used
mcqs.explain: Each participant receives two or more treatments.

mcqs.q: The purpose of the washout period is to:
opts: Remove the effects of the first treatment before the second one is started
Allow recruitment of additional participants
Blind the investigators
Increase the sample size
mcqs.explain: The two treatments could be two different active interventions, or one intervention and a placebo.

mcqs.q: The built-in advantage of the crossover design is that:
opts: Each participant acts as their own control, removing differences between people
It requires no randomization
It removes the need for a washout period
It eliminates the placebo effect
mcqs.explain: This is why crossover trials can answer the question with far fewer participants.

mcqs.q: Clinical trials are called the gold standard in medicine because:
opts: They give the greatest justification for concluding causality and are subject to the least number of problems or bias
They are the cheapest to run
They take the least time
They need the fewest participants
mcqs.explain: They are the basic design against which other designs are judged.

mcqs.q: Clinical trials are the best type of study when the objective is to:
opts: Establish the efficacy of a treatment or a procedure
Estimate the prevalence of a disease
Map what research already exists
Describe an unusual case
mcqs.explain: Randomized controlled trials are described as the strongest designs of all.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed as a disadvantage of clinical trials?
opts: They cannot establish causality
The inappropriate use of historical controls has led to serious errors in medicine
Great expense
They need a long time
mcqs.explain: Establishing causality is their greatest strength, not a weakness.

mcqs.q: The fourth listed disadvantage concerns practices that:
opts: Become established and accepted by the medical community even though they have not been properly justified
Are abandoned before being tested
Are too new to be studied
Are used only outside hospitals
mcqs.explain: Once a practice is widely believed to work, it becomes ethically difficult to randomize patients away from it.

mcqs.q: The hierarchy of evidence reflects the fact that:
opts: Different types of study have different levels of reliability and validity
Older studies are always less reliable
Larger studies are always better
Only randomized trials are valid
mcqs.explain: It groups the different types of study used in clinical research.

mcqs.q: Which sits at the APEX of the hierarchy of evidence?
opts: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses
Randomised controlled trials
Cohort studies
Case series and case reports
mcqs.explain: Ideas, editorials and opinions sit at the base.

mcqs.q: Which sits at the BASE of the hierarchy of evidence?
opts: Ideas, editorials and opinions
Case series and case reports
Ecological studies
Cross-sectional surveys
mcqs.explain: The order upward is ideas and opinions, case series and case reports, ecological studies, cross-sectional surveys, case-control, cohort, RCTs, then systematic reviews and meta-analyses.

mcqs.q: In the hierarchy of evidence, cohort studies sit:
opts: Above case-control studies and below randomised controlled trials
Below case-control studies
Above randomised controlled trials
At the same level as case reports
mcqs.explain: Ranking upward: cross-sectional surveys, case-control, cohort, RCTs.

mcqs.q: A systematic review is:
opts: An overview of a specific topic that attempts to cover all of the relevant high-quality research evidence
A statistical pooling of numerical results
A summary of one author's opinion of a field
A description of a series of similar cases
mcqs.explain: Its authors systematically search for, appraise and summarize all the relevant medical literature.

mcqs.q: A meta-analysis is:
opts: When the numerical data from many smaller studies are combined and analyzed statistically
A narrative summary of the literature
A single very large randomized trial
A qualitative appraisal of study quality
mcqs.explain: It is often included in a systematic review but can also be published on its own.

mcqs.q: The main benefit of a meta-analysis is that it:
opts: Can provide more precise estimates of the effects of health care than individual studies provide
Eliminates publication bias
Removes the need for a systematic search
Guarantees that the studies were well conducted
mcqs.explain: It analyses data from a number of independent studies on a similar topic and gives an estimate of an overall result.

mcqs.q: Regarding data type, a systematic review is ... whereas a meta-analysis is ...
opts: Qualitative and quantitative; strictly quantitative
Strictly quantitative; qualitative
Always qualitative; always narrative
Always narrative; always descriptive
mcqs.explain: The systematic review appraises and synthesises; the meta-analysis pools numbers.

mcqs.q: Which correctly states the relationship between the two?
opts: A systematic review is a method of reviewing; a meta-analysis is a statistical technique applied to the studies the review gathered
A meta-analysis always contains a systematic review
They are two names for the same thing
A systematic review can only be done after a meta-analysis
mcqs.explain: Every meta-analysis needs a systematic search behind it, but not every systematic review contains a meta-analysis.

mcqs.q: A listed limitation of the meta-analysis is that it is:
opts: Prone to publication bias and requires similar study designs
Unable to increase statistical power
Unable to give an effect size
Purely qualitative
mcqs.explain: Its strengths are increased statistical power, a precise effect size and resolution of conflicting results.

saqs.q: Define experimental research and list the four families of experimental design with their members.
saqs.a: Experimental research is a research design in which the researcher deliberately changes one or more conditions and observes the effect on an outcome; it is used to examine causal relationships, the researcher introducing a treatment, intervention, condition or stimulus and then measuring whether an outcome changes in response. This controlled change is what separates an experiment from many other forms of empirical research. The families are: pre-experimental, comprising the one-shot case study, the one-group pretest-posttest design and the static group design; true-experimental, comprising the pretest-posttest control group, the posttest-only control group and the Solomon four-group designs; statistical, comprising time series and multiple time series; and quasi-experimental, comprising randomized blocks, the Latin square and factorial design.

saqs.q: Describe the three pre-experimental designs and list the uses of pre-experimental design.
saqs.a: The one-shot case study design involves a single experimental group evaluated on a single occasion after they have experienced a specific event, treatment or intervention; all observations are conducted exclusively after the treatment has been implemented, subjects are not randomly assigned to the experimental group, and the design does not include a control group for comparison. The one-group pretest-posttest design is the simplest type of pre-experimental design; only the experimental group is selected as the study subjects, a pre-test of the dependent variable is conducted before the implementation of the treatment, and following the treatment a post-test is carried out to assess the overall effect, so the impact of the intervention is measured both before and after, but there is no control group. The static group comparison design uses two groups whose selection is non-randomized: group 1, the experimental group, is treated with the intervention X, while group 2, the control group, receives no intervention or business as usual; both then undergo post-test observation only, and a difference in post-test scores suggests the effect of the intervention. Pre-experimental designs are often the first step in the research process and can provide valuable insights that inform future studies; their uses are exploratory studies exploring a new area of study or phenomenon, pilot studies to test feasibility before conducting larger and more rigorous experiments, preliminary investigations between variables to provide initial evidence for the presence or absence of relationships, one-shot case studies giving preliminary evidence of the potential effects of an intervention, one-group pretest-posttest designs to examine changes within the group over time, time-series designs providing insight into how outcomes change over time by measuring the dependent variable at multiple time points before and after the intervention, feasibility studies assessing whether a larger-scale experimental study is practical and achievable given available resources and constraints, and educational research evaluating the effectiveness of teaching methods, interventions or programs in real-world settings.

saqs.q: Define true experimental design and describe its three types.
saqs.a: True experimental design employs random assignment, control groups and experimental groups to minimize bias and obtain credible results; participants are randomly assigned to experimental groups or control groups, and it is often called the gold standard of research because it helps organizations and researchers prove what really drives change. The pretest-posttest control group design measures the dependent variable before and after introducing the independent variable, with both the control and the experimental group tested and only the experimental group receiving the treatment. The posttest-only control group design randomly assigns participants to an experimental group receiving the active treatment or a control group receiving a placebo with no active ingredient, and takes only a post-test measurement after the treatment period, so that a difference between the groups establishes cause and effect. The Solomon four-group design combines pretest-posttest and posttest-only designs, using four groups, two with pretests and two without, which helps control for pretest effects and reveals both the effect of the research and whether taking a pre-survey influenced the response.

saqs.q: Define quasi-experimental design and explain how it differs from a true experiment.
saqs.a: Quasi-experimental design is used to estimate the causal impact of an intervention on a target population. Unlike true experimental designs, quasi-experiments lack random assignment of participants to experimental and control groups; instead, researchers work with pre-existing groups or natural cohorts, making them especially useful in real-world settings where randomization is impractical or unethical. For example, a study of a new teaching method may compare students from School A who use the new method with students from School B who do not; the measured outcomes such as test scores are compared between the groups, but because the groups were not randomly assigned and may differ in other ways such as prior knowledge or demographics, the results might show an effect while the certainty of that conclusion is limited.

saqs.q: Describe the randomized controlled trial, blinding, and the crossover trial.
saqs.a: In the randomized controlled trial, normal people are randomized so that one arm is given the intervention and the other is given nothing or a placebo, and both arms are then followed up to count who develops the outcome and who does not. Randomisation works by entering information about everyone taking part in the trial into a computer; the computer gives each participant a code number; the code numbers are randomly assigned to the different treatment arms, helping to prevent bias; and the control arm then receives the standard treatment while the test arm receives the new treatment. Blinding refers to patients and investigators, including those involved in recruitment and assessing the outcome, having no knowledge of treatment allocation; traditionally, blinded randomized controlled trials have been classified as single-blind, double-blind or triple-blind. In a crossover trial each participant receives two or more treatments; each subject usually receives two treatments in random order, often separated by what is called a washout period with no treatment. The washout period is usually included to remove the effects of the first treatment before the second one is started, and the two treatments could be two different active interventions, or one intervention and a placebo.

saqs.q: List the advantages and disadvantages of clinical trials.
saqs.a: The advantages are that clinical trials are the gold standard in medicine, that is, the basic design against which other designs are judged, because they give the greatest justification for concluding causality and are subject to the least number of problems or bias; that they are the best type of study to use when the objective is to establish the efficacy of a treatment or a procedure; and that randomized controlled trials are the strongest designs of all. The disadvantages are that the inappropriate use of historical controls has led to serious errors in medicine; the great expense; the need for a long time; and the problem that arises when certain practices become established and accepted by the medical community even though they have not been properly justified.

saqs.q: Explain the hierarchy of evidence and distinguish a systematic review from a meta-analysis.
saqs.a: The different types of study used in clinical research can be grouped into what is known as the hierarchy of evidence, which reflects the fact that different types of study have different levels of reliability and validity. From the base upward it runs: ideas, editorials and opinions; case series and case reports; ecological studies; cross-sectional surveys; case-control studies; cohort studies; randomised controlled trials; and, at the apex, systematic reviews and meta-analyses. A systematic review is an overview of a specific topic that attempts to cover all of the relevant high-quality research evidence; in it, the authors will have systematically searched for, appraised and summarized all of the medical literature that is relevant to that specific research question. A meta-analysis is often included in a systematic review but can also be published on its own; it is when the numerical data from many smaller studies are combined and analyzed statistically, so it analyses the data from a number of independent studies that are on a similar topic and gives an estimate of an overall result, and it can provide more precise estimates of the effects of health care than individual studies provide. In short, the systematic review is a method of reviewing and is qualitative and quantitative, while the meta-analysis is a statistical technique applied to the studies the review has gathered and is strictly quantitative.
